doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Katrina, gentrification and the loss of New Orleans' culture
summary: He recounts his angry letter to a journalist claiming the city is back, the Hastert remark, leisure time as the source of creativity, and the post-Katrina housing changes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Oh, I’m sorry, you’re right. So I wrote this scathing response saying that you know I mean listen, after Katrina happened the then-speaker of the house Denny Hastert actually said, “New Orleans is going to be too expensive to rebuild. If people want to hear jazz they can go to Walt Disney World.” Yeah he said that. The letter I wrote him I’m surprised I didn’t get a knock on the door from the Secret Service ‘cause it was pretty caustic. But the point is no, no, no. I mean here’s the thing. New Orleans — jazz was born of the confluence of the African diaspora and the European — New Orleans was the opera capital of the world, of the hemisphere in the 1700s. There was opera going on. You know there was African rhythms going on. Those two combined, people risked going to jail because integration was against the law and musicians were routinely, when they were caught jamming together, rounded up by the police and sent to jail. The point is the energy of New Orleans is what created its art. Katrina — I guess here’s the thing — I was asking a post-conviction capital defense attorney — last American heroes left —

why music flourished in New Orleans, why the creativity? She said, that’s easy, leisure time. In New Orleans, I mean it’s not called “The Big Easy” for nothing. And you know you could always go by so-and-so mama’s house who got some gumbo on the stove and you could make zero dollars in New Orleans and eat just fine. So people hung out, they hung out with each other and they shedded and they created, you know, music, like Ellis Marsalis, the quintet, the early quintet. They — James Black. They influenced Coltrane and his quartet when they came and hung in New Orleans. They influenced — there was a great tenor player named Nat Perrilliat who was playing sheets of sound while Coltrane was still playing two fives. And you know New Orleans has an incredible power, like even to this day. And I’m sorry this is kind of rambling all over the map answer, but even to this day there’s a soul food restaurant on Esplanade called Lil Dizzy’s Café, owned by the Baquet family. One of their sons is Dean Baquet, the editor of the New York Times. We have influence — the culture informs on a global level. And what happened during Katrina was this indigenous, rich heritage of multiple generations of French, Spanish, African-American, Italian, Irish, all of these people had their neighborhoods and they interacted with each other. And most of the white people were raised by black people. There was a separation of the races but there was a communing of the races you know, informally, both artistically and socially. After Katrina all of that leisure time that I spoke of earlier, that went away, because predatory investors came in and bought up all the housing stock, fixed up all the houses. The rents became Manhattan-level rents, and the salaries did not follow. So the indigenous people, the people who sat on the front stoop checking out the latest Sonny Stitt record wondering how that fit in and trying to cop the notes, those people suddenly had to work two or three jobs just to afford the place they lived in all their lives. And it was a cultural genocide. So I didn’t have any patience for the writer that said, “Oh I’m writing a piece about how it’s all back now.” No it’s not. Now I understand all culture erodes. I understand that. Culture changes. You know when I came out as a kid it was like man, I was playing with Danny Barker on Bourbon Street for six hours then I’d go play a bebop gig with James Black and Earl Turpentine after. And then at six in the morning we’d go to somebody’s house and shed ‘til noon. It was like amazing. And I said wow, this is really — and the old cats were saying this ain’t nothing like it used to be. Man we used to be this and this and this. Now you know kids go on Frenchman Street and play for the door, and mostly out of town musicians that are playing 20s and 30s swing music that tourists think is New Orleans traditional music. They don’t know the difference. Incidentally, a side note, the difference, we never call it Dixieland because of the word Dixie, and because Dixieland music didn’t start in New Orleans.
